atoms.text: The grief chatbot: a service reconstructs a dead partner from social media and messages, so mourning is automated.
The dead can be simulated from their digital traces: online behavior is enough to produce a convincing copy, so privacy ends at death.
The synthetic body: the chatbot is installed in an android that looks like the dead man, so grief becomes a physical relationship.
The widow and the copy: the protagonist cannot accept the android because it lacks the dead man's flaws, so love is defined by imperfection.
The copy that is too agreeable: the simulation omits negative traits, so comfort becomes uncanny and the dead are sanitized.
The pregnancy: the widow discovers she is carrying the dead man's child, so the copy competes with a future the original never saw.
The friend who recommends the service: a well-meaning friend signs her up, so grief is mediated by social pressure.
The service's experimental stage: the copy is a beta product, so the bereaved are also test subjects.
Letting go as the real task: the story asks whether simulation helps or prevents mourning, so technology is judged by its effect on grief.
The cliff: the widow orders the android to jump, so the fantasy of the dead is tested by an act of violence.
The remote country house: the couple's isolation makes the copy the only company, so the setting amplifies dependence.
The sister who is neglected: the widow stops answering her living family, so the dead displace the living.
The uploaded videos: photos and videos are fed to the system to improve the copy, so memory is a training set.
The ethics of the comfort object: the android satisfies sexual and emotional needs, so the story refuses to dismiss the copy as fake.
The quiet domestic scale: the sci-fi premise is staged as a grief drama, so the technology is measured in intimate gestures.
The dead as data: identity is reduced to a behavioral archive, so the story asks what part of a person cannot be downloaded.
